Trying to Conceive

When to Seek Fertility Help: 6 and 12 Month Guidelines

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Seek fertility help after 12 months of regular unprotected sex if you are under 35, after 6 months if you are 35 to 39, and right away if you are 40 or older. Those timelines, used by groups like ACOG, are a signal to start checking, not a diagnosis. And if your history already includes irregular periods, pelvic conditions, repeated miscarriage, or known male-factor issues, you do not need to wait for any calendar milestone.

The 6 and 12 month guidelines, explained

The mainstream medical advice is consistent. If you are under 35, seek a fertility evaluation after 12 months of regular, unprotected sex without a pregnancy. If you are 35 to 39, seek help after 6 months. If you are 40 or older, it is reasonable to ask for an evaluation as soon as you decide to try, without waiting at all. Regular here means sex every two to three days across the cycle, or timed around your fertile window, with no contraception of any kind. Months where you were apart, using condoms, or not actually trying do not count toward the total.

These thresholds exist because age affects how quickly an evaluation becomes worthwhile, not because anything dramatic changes on a birthday. Egg supply and egg quality decline gradually with age, so the cost of waiting a full year is higher at 38 than at 28. The timelines come from groups like ACOG and the American Society for Reproductive Medicine, and they mark the point where checking makes sense, not the point where something is wrong. Plenty of people who reach the 6 or 12 month mark go on to conceive, some without any treatment at all. Think of the timeline as an appointment trigger, not a verdict.

Reasons not to wait for the calendar

Some situations justify an evaluation now, no matter how long you have been trying. Book an appointment without waiting if your periods are irregular, very far apart, or absent, because that pattern often means ovulation is not happening reliably. The same applies if you have known or suspected endometriosis, known or suspected blocked or damaged fallopian tubes, a history of pelvic inflammatory disease or another pelvic infection, or previous surgery on your ovaries, tubes, uterus, or abdomen. These conditions can affect conception in ways that time alone will not fix, and finding out early gives you more options.

The do-not-wait list also includes two or more miscarriages, past cancer treatment such as chemotherapy or radiation for either partner, and known or suspected male-factor issues, for example a history of testicular surgery, significant injury, undescended testes, or trouble with erections or ejaculation. Fertility involves two people, so either partner's history counts. Pain with sex that makes regular intercourse difficult is also a valid reason to be seen sooner, both for comfort and for conception. If any of this sounds like you, you are not skipping the line by booking now. The timelines are meant for people with no known risk factors.

Help starts at a familiar office

You do not need to find a fertility clinic to get started. For most people, the first stop is a familiar one: your OB/GYN, midwife, or family doctor. When you book, say plainly that you have been trying to conceive for a certain number of months and would like a fertility evaluation, so the office schedules enough time. If you have a partner, it helps for both of you to come, since the evaluation covers both of you from the start. Beginning with a clinician who already knows your history keeps the first step small, local, and much less intimidating than the word fertility suggests.

Expect the first visit to be mostly conversation. A clinician will ask about your cycle history, past pregnancies for either partner, how long you have been trying, how often you are having sex, past contraception, medical conditions, medications and supplements, surgeries, infections, smoking, alcohol, and relevant family history. None of this requires special preparation beyond honest answers, and no question is meant to assign blame. Based on that history, the clinician will suggest which tests make sense first and in what order. If something in the workup later points toward specialist care, your doctor can arrange a referral, and that step has its own separate path.

What a first fertility evaluation involves

A basic evaluation looks at three questions: are eggs being released, is sperm present and healthy, and can egg and sperm meet. Confirming ovulation often starts with your cycle history and may include a blood test timed to a specific point in your cycle. A semen analysis checks the male side and is one of the simplest, highest-yield tests in the entire workup, which is why clinicians order it early rather than last. Depending on your history, imaging may be added: usually a pelvic ultrasound, and sometimes a specialized X-ray or saline ultrasound that checks whether the fallopian tubes are open.

Bloodwork can round out the picture. Depending on your age and symptoms, a clinician may check thyroid function, prolactin, and sometimes hormone markers that reflect ovarian reserve. Most of this testing is spread over one or two cycles, since some tests need to happen on particular cycle days. Two outcomes are common and both are useful: the evaluation finds a specific, often treatable issue, or it finds nothing alarming and you get reassurance plus a clearer plan. Ask at each step what the result would change, so the testing always feels connected to a decision rather than an open-ended search.

How to get ready, and how to steady yourself

A little preparation makes the first appointment far more productive. Bring the start dates of your last several periods and your typical cycle length, a list of medications and supplements for both partners, any relevant surgical or infection history, and roughly when you started trying. If you have been tracking ovulation signs, bring those notes too, but do not delay the appointment to gather perfect data. Writing down your top three questions in advance protects them from being forgotten in the moment. You can keep dates, symptoms, and questions in BeMama or in a simple notebook; what matters is having them in one place.

It is normal to feel a knot in your stomach about this appointment. Try to hold two ideas at once: asking for help early is not overreacting, and needing the full 12 months is not failing. A fertility evaluation is closer to a checkup than a verdict, and many people who go through one conceive, with or without treatment. If waiting is weighing on you, tell the clinician that too, since emotional strain is a legitimate part of the picture. A few symptoms should skip every timeline: sudden, severe pelvic pain needs urgent or emergency care the same day, especially if there is any chance you are pregnant, and very heavy bleeding or periods that stop for three months in a row deserve a prompt call to a clinician rather than waiting.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Fertility evaluation considers both partners and may include cycle history, ovulation, semen analysis, medicines, health conditions, imaging, or other tests. Timing for evaluation depends on age, how long pregnancy has been attempted, cycle regularity, and known reproductive factors.

Earlier advice can be appropriate when periods are absent or very irregular, pelvic disease or cancer treatment may affect fertility, or either partner has a known concern. A specialist determines which tests are useful; home tracking alone cannot diagnose infertility.

How BeMama can help

Bring a concise BeMama record of cycle dates, test results, symptoms, medicines, and how long you have been trying. It can make the history easier to explain without replacing a clinical evaluation.

When to seek help

Seek prompt care for severe pelvic pain, very heavy bleeding, or another urgent symptom instead of waiting for a fertility appointment.

Sources and further reading

  • ACOG — Evaluating Infertility
  • CDC — Infertility: Frequently Asked Questions

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Key takeaways

  • If you are under 35, seek fertility help after 12 months of trying; at 35 to 39, after 6 months; at 40 or older, right away.
  • Skip the timeline entirely if you have irregular periods, pelvic conditions, repeated miscarriage, cancer treatment history, or male-factor concerns.
  • Start with your regular OB/GYN, midwife, or family doctor, not a fertility clinic.
  • A first evaluation covers both partners: history, ovulation checks, a semen analysis, and basic imaging.
  • Meeting a timeline is a reason to check, not a sign that something is wrong.

Frequently asked questions

How long should you try to conceive before seeing a doctor?

Try for 12 months before seeing a doctor if you are under 35, and for 6 months if you are 35 to 39; at 40 or older, see a doctor as soon as you start trying. These timelines assume regular unprotected sex and no known fertility risk factors. If your periods are irregular or you have a relevant medical history, book an appointment now instead of watching the calendar.

We have been trying to conceive for 6 months with no luck. Should we see someone?

Yes, book a fertility evaluation now if the partner trying to carry the pregnancy is 35 or older, or if either of you has a known risk factor such as irregular cycles, pelvic conditions, or male-factor concerns. If the partner trying to carry is under 35, with regular cycles and no red flags for either of you, six months without a pregnancy is still common and not by itself a sign of a problem. Keep trying and use the 12 month mark as your appointment trigger. Booking earlier for peace of mind is also a reasonable choice, not an overreaction.

What does a fertility evaluation involve?

A first fertility evaluation usually involves a detailed health history for both partners, tests to confirm ovulation, a semen analysis, and basic imaging such as a pelvic ultrasound, with a tube check added when your history suggests it. Blood tests for thyroid function and certain hormones are often included. Testing is typically spread over one or two menstrual cycles because some tests are timed to specific cycle days.

When should I get fertility testing?

Get fertility testing after 12 months of trying if you are under 35, after 6 months if you are 35 to 39, and right away if you are 40 or older. Get tested sooner at any age if you have irregular or absent periods, endometriosis, tubal disease, a history of pelvic infection or surgery, two or more miscarriages, past cancer treatment, or known male-factor issues. Your regular doctor or OB/GYN can order the first round of tests.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
